```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(bayesEfron.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
big <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")
megabytes <- function(draws, variables) round(draws * variables * 8 / 2^20)
```

If you report results from bayesEfron, you may be asked whether the fit
can be reproduced and what evidence there is that its intervals have their
nominal coverage. Here we collect what you need to answer: how to
reproduce a fit, what a fitted object stores, the two Stan programs, the
checks that we ran on the computations, interval coverage in simulated
data, and how the package relates to the paper [@lee2025].

```{r library}
library(bayesEfron)
```

Our example is `krw_fit`, a fit that comes with the package. It is the fit
to the callback gaps of 97 firms that `vignette("bayesEfron")` analyzes.

```{r stored-fit}
fit <- krw_fit
```

## Reproducing a fit

A fitted object records what produced its draws. We first print the seed,
the CmdStan version, the name of the Stan program and the first characters
of a hash of the program's file.

```{r reproduce}
fit$metadata$seed
fit$metadata$cmdstan_version
attr(fit$metadata, "program")
substr(fit$metadata$stan_file_sha256, 1, 12)
```

If you do not set `seed` in `bayes_efron_fit()`, the sampler's seed is
taken from the clock, and it is stored either way. Of the two Stan
programs, which are described below, `efron_mix` is the default.

The sampler settings are stored as an attribute of `metadata`, and so are
the bayesEfron and cmdstanr versions that made the fit.

```{r sampler-settings}
settings <- attr(fit$metadata, "sampler_settings")
str(settings[c("chains", "iter_warmup", "iter_sampling", "adapt_delta",
               "max_treedepth", "init")])
attr(fit$metadata, "package_version")
attr(fit$metadata, "cmdstanr_version")
```

Another attribute is the grid, stored as `make_efron_grid()` returned it,
together with the method that chose its range. By default this is
`"pilot"`, which fits the model once on a wide range before it sets the
limits of the grid. Because this pilot fit runs with the seed of the call,
the grid is reproduced along with the rest.

```{r grid}
grid <- attr(fit$metadata, "grid")
grid$grid_method
grid$support
str(grid$pilot[c("narrowed", "seed", "iter_warmup", "iter_sampling")])
```

```{r reproduce-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(attr(fit$metadata, "program"), "efron_mix"),
          identical(grid$grid_method, "pilot"), grid$pilot$seed == fit$metadata$seed,
          isFALSE(grid$pilot$narrowed),
          all(c("theta_hat", "sigma", "grid", "B") %in% names(fit$metadata$data_list)))
```

Here the pilot fit used the same seed as the fit and did not narrow the
range.

Finally, `fit$metadata$data_list` contains the data and the spline basis.
If you use the same data, settings, seed and versions on the same machine,
you get the same draws. On another machine or with another CmdStan version
the draws can differ, and the results then agree only to within Monte
Carlo error.

## Stored draws and the size of a fit

By default a fit stores the draws of the spline coefficients, `lambda` and
$g$, with five quantities computed from them, and nothing for the sites.
Every site summary is computed from the draws of $g$ when a method needs
it, as `vignette("model")` describes, so the size of a fit does not grow
with the number of sites.

The dimensions of the draws and the `storage` attribute show what the
example fit contains.

```{r kept}
dim(fit$draws)
str(attr(fit$metadata, "storage")[c("site_draws", "iterations", "chains",
                                    "thin")])
```

```{r kept-facts, include = FALSE}
variables <- dim(fit$draws)[3]
K <- nobs(fit)
stopifnot(variables == 114L, K == 97L, dim(twin_towers_fit$draws)[3] == 116L,
          megabytes(12000, variables) == 10, megabytes(12000, variables + 5 * K) == 55,
          megabytes(12000, 116 + 5 * 1500) > 650)
```

We made the example fit with `thin = 15`, so it has
`r prod(dim(fit$draws)[1:2])` draws of `r variables` variables. Without
thinning the same fit has 12,000 draws, which take about
`r megabytes(12000, variables)` megabytes. A fit made with
`site_draws = TRUE` also stores five variables for each site, as version
0.3.0 did, and its 12,000 draws take about
`r megabytes(12000, variables + 5 * K)` megabytes for the 97 firms and
about `r big(megabytes(12000, 116 + 5 * 1500))` megabytes for 1,500 sites.
These sizes are for the draws alone, and the fitted object as a whole is a
little larger.

Thinning only reduces what is stored. The sampler diagnostics still
describe the whole run, as `vignette("diagnostics")` explains. You can
also store the cmdstanr fit object, with `keep_cmdstan_fit = TRUE`, but it
refers to temporary files and is only useful in the session that created
it.

### Fits saved by earlier versions

A fit that was saved by an earlier version of the package can still be
used, although it may lack some of the attributes described above. If its
table of site effects or its `effective_params` was computed under earlier
definitions, the methods compute them again from the stored draws of $g$
and issue a warning, and the saved object is not changed (see `?bef_fit`).
A saved result of `summary()` contains no draws, so it cannot be updated
in this way: `print()` throws an error that asks you to call `summary()`
again on the fit. For a fit saved by the first released version, 0.1.0,
`diagnose()`, `predict()` and `loo()` are not available and throw an
error.

## Two Stan programs

bayesEfron contains two Stan programs. To read them, find the files with
`system.file()`:

```{r stan-file, eval = FALSE}
system.file("stan", "efron_mix.stan", package = "bayesEfron")
system.file("stan", "efron_re.stan", package = "bayesEfron")
```

The default program is `efron_mix.stan`, and its comments state the model
that `vignette("model")` describes. It allows a normal component at each
grid point, computes the likelihood of all the sites as one matrix
product, and writes nothing for the sites.

The other program, `efron_re.stan`, is the program of version 0.3.0. We
have left it as it was, and a test in the package checks that the file
has the same hash as the released one. For a $g$ with point masses the
two programs describe the same model, and a test checks that their fits
of the callback data agree within Monte Carlo error.

Each program is compiled the first time it is needed, and the compiled
model is stored in your user cache directory and reused in later sessions.
Its file name includes a hash of the Stan file, the CmdStan version and
the machine architecture, so the program is compiled again when the Stan
file or the CmdStan version changes. See `?bayes_efron_compile` for where
the directory is and how to clear it.

### Reproducing a result of version 0.3.0

To obtain a result of version 0.3.0 again, set `settings = "0.3.0"`. The
fit then runs `efron_re.stan` with the grid method, the 101 grid points
and the site-level draws of that version:

```{r settings-030, eval = FALSE}
bayes_efron_fit(raudenbush1985, seed = 1985, settings = "0.3.0")
```

For the same seed this gives the draws of version 0.3.0, provided that the
CmdStan version, the compiler and the machine are the same as well.
Another CmdStan version can change the draws, and also the number of
digits with which they are written.

The current program writes its draws with `r settings$sig_figs`
significant digits, and the site summaries are computed from the draws of
$g$ (see above), so estimates far from zero need no centering. In a fit
with `settings = "0.3.0"`, however, the site-level draws are written with
CmdStan's default number of digits (8 in recent versions). They lose the
digits in which the sites differ when the estimates are about 10 million
times their standard errors or more, so center such estimates first.

For a fit made with `settings = "0.3.0"`, the summaries follow the
definitions of the current version. To get the interval limits as version
0.3.0 computed them, use `confint(method = "draws")`.

## The data and the stored results

The vignettes use three data sets, each with a stored fit (`krw_fit`,
`twin_towers_fit` and `raudenbush_fit`).

- `krw_discrimination` contains the callback gaps of 97 firms from the
  experiment of @kline2022. It uses the sample of @kline2024, and we
  recomputed the estimates from the replication files of @walters2024.
- `twin_towers` is one simulated data set with 1,500 sites from the
  simulation study of @lee2025, taken from that study's files.
- `raudenbush1985` contains the 19 studies of @raudenbush1985.

A fourth data set, `star_schools`, has the estimated effects of small
classes in the 79 schools of Tennessee's Project STAR. The case study
that analyzes it is an article on the package website, and its fit is not
installed with the package.

See each data set's help page for its source.

We made the fits with `data-raw/example-fits.R` in the source repository,
using the defaults (with 8 spline functions for the simulated sites) and
fixed seeds. The script runs each fit with all 12,000 draws and thins it
to 1 draw in 15. It then compares the site intervals from the thinned
draws with the intervals from all the draws, and it fails with an error if
a fit has not converged or an interval limit moves by more than 2 grid
spacings.

```{r kept-facts-2, include = FALSE}
evidence <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "lee_sui_examples.rds",
                                package = "bayesEfron"))$cases$twin
# The probability of a positive effect, read on the grid points: from the
# kept draws and from all the draws of the same run.
kept_draws <- unname(exceedance_prob(twin_towers_fit, reading = "step"))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(kept_draws, evidence$positive_probability)),
          length(evidence$full_positive_probability) == 1500L,
          max(abs(kept_draws - evidence$full_positive_probability)) < 0.005)
largest_change <- max(abs(kept_draws - evidence$full_positive_probability))
```

For the simulated sites we also compared the probability that a site's
effect is positive, read on the grid points (`reading = "step"`), between
the thinned draws and all the draws. It differs by at most
`r num(largest_change, 4)`.

No model is fitted when the documentation is built. The vignettes read
these fits and the files in `inst/examples` and `inst/verification`, and
both directories have a README that names the script that made every file.

## Checks against known answers

The checks in this section are tests in the package's test suite
(`tests/testthat` in the source repository), so they are run again
whenever the package is checked. The tests that sample need CmdStan.

The tests check the package's computations in two steps. In the first
step the model's formulas, written out in plain R, are compared with
results obtained in another way:

- the posterior distribution of a site effect under a normal $g$, with the
  conjugate normal result
- the mean and variance of $g$, with Gauss-Hermite quadrature
- the posterior mode, with a numerical optimizer

In the second step the quantities that each Stan program writes are
recomputed from the spline coefficients with those R formulas, and the
two are compared.

With a single normal component the default program is the normal model,
so another test samples from it in that case and checks that the result
agrees with the normal model. For the spline basis the package calls
`splines::ns(grid, df = M, intercept = FALSE)`, and a test checks that it
uses the result unchanged. If the columns of the basis and a constant
column are not linearly independent, `make_efron_grid()` throws an error.

Other tests compare fits with deconvolveR, the implementation by
@narasimhan2020 of the empirical Bayes estimator of @efron2016, on three
simulated data sets with equal standard errors and 20, 50 and 100 sites.
We do not expect the two methods to coincide, so the tests only require
them to be close: the posterior means of the site effects within one
standard error of the deconvolveR estimates, with a correlation of at
least 0.99, and the two estimates of $g$ for the largest data set within
0.25 in total variation distance.

These tests show that the pieces are computed correctly. They do not show
that the intervals have the right coverage, which only simulated data
can.

## Interval coverage in simulated data

Whether 90% intervals contain the true effects 90% of the time can only be
checked where the true effects are known. We fitted three sets of
simulated data with the defaults, and the code below collects the stored
results in one table.

```{r coverage}
verification <- function(name) {
  read.csv(system.file("verification", name, package = "bayesEfron"),
           check.names = FALSE)
}
panels <- verification("panels-methods.csv")
panels <- panels[panels$method == "bayesEfron", ]
few <- verification("few-studies.csv")
few <- few[few$method == "bayesEfron", ]
equal <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "ebnm_comparison.rds",
                             package = "bayesEfron"))$equal_se$repeated
equal <- equal[equal$method == "bayesEfron" & equal$M == 6, ]

checked <- data.frame(
  effects = c("two groups", "two groups", paste("19 studies,", few$scenario),
              "two groups, equal standard errors"),
  sites = c(panels$K, rep(19, nrow(few)), 1500),
  data_sets = c(panels$panels, few$replications, equal$panels),
  inclusion = c(panels$inclusion, few$inclusion, equal$inclusion),
  se = c(panels$inclusion_se, few$inclusion_se, equal$inclusion_se)
)
checked[c("inclusion", "se")] <- round(checked[c("inclusion", "se")], 3)
checked
```

```{r coverage-facts, include = FALSE}
unequal <- checked[-nrow(checked), ]
last <- checked[nrow(checked), ]
stopifnot(nrow(checked) == 6L, identical(panels$K, c(100L, 1500L)),
          identical(panels$panels, c(100L, 20L)), all(few$replications == 200L),
          equal$panels == 20,
          all(abs(unequal$inclusion - 0.9) <= 0.008),
          all(abs(unequal$inclusion - 0.9) < 2 * unequal$se),
          last$inclusion < 0.88, (0.9 - last$inclusion) / last$se > 3)
print(range(unequal$inclusion))
```

In this table, `inclusion` is the proportion of the true effects that lie
inside the 90% intervals of `site_summary()`, averaged over the data sets.
It estimates the coverage of those intervals, and `se` is its Monte Carlo
standard error. There are three simulation designs.

- In rows 1 and 2, every data set has its own true effects, which we
  simulated from two separate groups: a third of the sites between $-1.7$
  and $-0.7$, and two thirds between $0.7$ and $2.7$. These are the
  populations of the simulation study of @lee2025. The standard errors are
  unequal, and the largest is 9 times the smallest.
- Rows 3 to 5 are the data sets from `vignette("teacher-expectancy")`,
  which have the standard errors of the 19 studies and true effects from
  three distributions.
- In row 6, the true effects of the 20 large data sets in row 2 are each
  estimated with a standard error of 1.

In the five rows with unequal standard errors the coverage is between
`r num(min(unequal$inclusion), 3)` and `r num(max(unequal$inclusion), 3)`,
which is within two standard errors of 0.90 in each row. When every
standard error is equal to 1, however, it is `r num(last$inclusion, 3)`.
The fits in that row converged, and we have not isolated the cause of
the shortfall. See `vignette("empirical-bayes")` for what is known about
it and what it means in practice.

We also fitted the 20 large data sets in row 2 with 8 spline functions and
with `settings = "0.3.0"`. The next table compares the three settings.

```{r convergence}
convergence <- verification("panels-convergence.csv")
data.frame(setting = convergence$setting, valid = convergence$valid,
           rhat_max = round(convergence$rhat_max, 3),
           ess_bulk_min = round(convergence$ess_bulk_min),
           treedepth_share_max = round(convergence$treedepth_share_max, 3),
           seconds = round(convergence$sampling_seconds_median),
           inclusion = round(convergence$inclusion, 3))
```

```{r convergence-facts, include = FALSE}
defaults <- convergence[convergence$setting == "defaults", ]
eight <- convergence[convergence$setting == "M = 8", ]
old <- convergence[grepl("0.3.0", convergence$setting, fixed = TRUE), ]
stopifnot(all(convergence$panels == 20), defaults$valid == 20, eight$valid == 20,
          old$valid < 10, old$rhat_max > 1.05, defaults$rhat_max < 1.01,
          defaults$divergences == 0, old$sampling_seconds_median >
            3 * defaults$sampling_seconds_median,
          defaults$pilot_seconds_median > 20, old$pilot_seconds_median == 0,
          eight$sampling_seconds_median < defaults$sampling_seconds_median,
          (0.9 - eight$inclusion) / eight$inclusion_se > 2)
```

Here `valid` counts the fits that meet three conditions: the largest R-hat
over `alpha`, `lambda` and the mean and standard deviation of $g$ is below
1.01, the smallest bulk effective sample size is at least 400, and there
is no divergent transition. The next three columns give the worst case
among the 20 fits, and `seconds` is the median sampling time.

All `r defaults$valid` fits with the defaults meet the three conditions.
Sampling takes a median of `r round(defaults$sampling_seconds_median)`
seconds, after `r round(defaults$pilot_seconds_median)` seconds for the
pilot fit that sets the range. With `settings = "0.3.0"`, `r old$valid` of
the 20 fits meet them, and sampling takes
`r round(old$sampling_seconds_median)` seconds. Sampling is fastest with 8
spline functions, but the intervals from those fits have a coverage of
`r num(eight$inclusion, 3)`, more than two standard errors below 0.90.
`vignette("diagnostics")` uses the same table to discuss what the
diagnostics do and do not measure.

These simulations cover one shape of $g$ with many sites and three shapes
with few sites, two patterns of unequal standard errors, and normal errors
with known standard errors. They do not cover numbers of sites other than
19, 100 and 1,500, standard errors that are themselves poorly estimated,
or effects that are related to their standard errors. You can
find the scripts in `data-raw/benchmark/` in the source repository, and
`inst/verification/README.md` describes the columns of the tables.

## Relation to the paper

bayesEfron implements the fully Bayesian model of @lee2025 [Section 4].
The table shows how the paper's quantities are written in the package.

| Paper | Package | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $\Theta_i$ | $\theta_i$ in the documentation | True effect of site $i$ |
| $\hat\theta_i$, $\sigma_i$ | `theta_hat`, `sigma` | Estimate and its standard error |
| $\mathcal{T} = \{\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\}$ | `grid`, with `L` points $\tau_j$ | Grid on which $g$ is defined |
| $Q$, an $m \times p$ matrix | `B`, an `L` by `M` matrix | Spline basis on the grid |
| $\alpha$, $\lambda$ | `alpha`, `lambda` | Spline coefficients and their prior precision |
| $g_j$ | `exp(log_g)` | Probability of grid point $j$ |
| $\pi_{ij}$ | $w_{ij}$ in `vignette("model")`; not stored | Posterior probability of grid point $j$ for site $i$, given $\alpha$ |

In three places the package's defaults differ from the paper, and each can
be changed back to the paper's choice.

1. In the code of the paper's application, the grid covers the range of
   the estimates extended by half its width on each side, which is
   `grid_method = "paper_realdata"`. The default method, `"pilot"`, starts
   from that range and narrows it where the pilot fit shows that $g$
   occupies only a part of it, but it never widens it. See
   `vignette("choosing-a-grid")` for details.
2. The number of grid points is 101 unless the smallest standard error or
   the spread of the estimates is small compared with the grid spacing, in
   which case more points are used. Set `L = 101` to keep 101 points.
3. The paper obtains the site intervals as quantiles of posterior draws of
   the effects (its Appendix B.4), and so did version 0.3.0 of the
   package. We now compute them from the posterior distribution itself,
   with the probability of each grid point spread over its grid cell. In
   `site_summary()`, `reading = "step"` leaves the probabilities on the
   points, and a fit made with `site_draws = TRUE` gives the intervals
   from draws with `confint(method = "draws")`.

To restore the first two at once, use `settings = "0.3.0"`, which also
stores the site-level draws. The other two grid methods,
`"paper_simulation"` and `"paper_sensitivity"`, are the methods that the
code accompanying the paper,
<https://github.com/joonho112/fully-bayes-efron-prior>, uses for its
simulation study and its sensitivity analysis. Where the paper's text and
its code differ in a detail, the package follows the code. For example,
the paper's Stan appendix shows a grid that extends 0.5 units beyond the
estimates on each side, whereas the simulation code builds the grid from
the true effects.

`confint()` can also return the shortest interval with posterior
probability `level` (`interval = "hpd"`). For point masses it is the
shortest interval after the probability of each grid point has been
spread evenly over one grid spacing around it, and where a range of
intervals is equally short, the middle one is returned. For normal
components the limits are moved until no nearby interval with that
probability is shorter, and the length of the result is within one
hundredth of the length of the shortest interval. In both cases the
interval has probability `level` exactly. With `method = "draws"`, and
always for `type = "g"`, it is the shortest interval that contains at
least that proportion of the draws.

The package also has features that are not in the paper:

- the normal components
- the `"pilot"` method for the range, and what `diagnose()` reports about
  the grid
- the effective number of parameters
- the log likelihood of each site and the cross-validation built on it
- `predict()`
- the plots

The table of site effects follows the paper's definitions
[@lee2025, Section 4.3 and Appendix A]: the posterior mean, the posterior
standard deviation with both parts of the variance, the posterior mode on
the grid, and an interval of the stated probability, which the package
takes with equal tails.

To cite the package, please cite the paper. You can get the reference with
`citation("bayesEfron")`.
